title: Is a control bigger than the target zone enough to reproduce run A's oscillation?
question: Does always turning a terminal dial with a long hold (run A's habit) make tuning oscillate, even for a policy that reads the match trend correctly?
hypothesis: Control size alone decides whether terminal tuning converges. A policy that follows the match trend perfectly but always uses a long hold (≈ 20% of the dial, wider than the ≈ 7% aligned zone) will overshoot again and again and fail to lock the terminals within the episode; the same policy with graded turns will lock all four.

motivation.observation: Live run A stopped after 473 decisions alternating dial up / dial down at the Harmony terminal. The fix for run B added three assists at once (trend_inference, hold_still_rule, control_magnitudes), so the run cannot say which one mattered. This experiment isolates the control-size half of the failure with a scripted policy, where the direction rule is held perfect.
evidence: docs/NEXT_MODEL.md §1: run A, 473 decisions oscillating at Harmony
src/game/afterhours/puzzle.ts: aligned tolerance 0.035 (≈ 7% of the dial wide), a 0.9 s hold ramps to ≈ 20%
scripts/capture-probes.ts: the heavy-handed (always long) baseline was needed to produce the overshoot probe

conditions.label: Always a long hold (run A's habit)

successCriteria: long fails to lock all four terminals in most seeded runs, with many overshoots, while graded locks all four
tap converges, but only by paying many more inputs than graded
falsificationCriteria: long locks all four terminals as reliably as graded: control size alone does not explain run A, and the direction/hold-still half deserves the attention
long overshoots fewer than 10 more times than graded (median, paired)
limitations: A scripted policy with a perfect direction rule, not a model: it isolates what the task does to one habit, not whether Jev has the habit.
Latency is resampled from one live run's 212 recorded latencies.
